433.dq: De grondwoorden, die in het B. nooit minder dan twee lettergrepen tellen, hebben den klemtoon op de voorlaatste syllabe ... In inekoe 'mijne moeder' toont het accent op i aan, dat het woord wordt gevoeld als ine + koe; werd het als een nieuw geheel beschouwd, dan zou het met den klemtoon op ne worden uitgesproken.
433.prule: Stress (realized as a pitch rise) on the penultimate syllable of the stem (grondwoord; stems are minimally disyllabic). Prefixes never move it; of the living suffixes only disyllabic -aka takes the main stress (on its penult, the stem stress surviving as secondary); all other suffixes and the enclitics mo, pa, dja leave stress on the stem penult (inekoe 'my mother' stressed on i; B. ánanja vs Todjo anánja). The echo-vowel final syllable (-i after an original final consonant) does not count (kobati on ko). Dead suffixes -a/-ani, -o/-oni and the old article -e shifted stress one syllable rightward in the words they formed; -sa sometimes shifts, sometimes not.
433.srule: Secondary stress (bijtoon) is stated in two places. (i) -aka derivations: main stress on the penult of -aka, the stem's own penult stress kept as bijtoon: tetendelaka, nakitasaka, koedongesaka (par. 4 p. 24). (ii) A syllable standing two places before the stressed syllable carries a bijtoon (par. 3 p. 19: mengkojoejoe, mendjololo, mentoemboli); par. 40 p. 86 states that a derived word of four or more syllables has a bijtoon on the fourth syllable from the end, because that syllable stands two places before the main stress (me'ajoeta, ke'alinta, mo'aloebiroe). For long prefix strings (3-5 prefixes) a main-plus-secondary pattern (secondary on the pa before p/mp) is conceivable, but usually (gewoonlijk) the voice simply rises gradually to the stressed syllable and then falls (par. 4 p. 24).

454.srule: None: one stressed (final) syllable per word; all non-final (pre-tonic) syllables are unstressed and bear only high tone ('an unstressed syllable is any non-final syllable with high tone. 454.quote: Polysyllabic words in CLZ have final stress. Final syllables tend to be heavy CVC syllables although they may be light CV syllables. tn.quote: Cada palabra del triqui tiene su tono, es decir, una melodía que forma una parte integral de la palabra. El triqui tiene cinco niveles de tono; podemos escribirlos con números ... 1 2 3 4 5. Los tonos 4 y 5 siempre se pronuncian como deslices. ... También existen tres patrones más que son combinaciones de dos niveles. Una de estas combinaciones empieza en el nivel 1 y sube al nivel 3; otra empieza en el nivel 3 y baja al nivel 1; y otra empieza en el nivel 3 y baja al nivel 2. Estas tres combinaciones se indican con los números 1-3, 3-1 y 3-2.
tn.translation: Every Triqui word has its tone, that is, a melody that forms an integral part of the word. Triqui has five tone levels; we can write them with numbers ... 1 2 3 4 5. Tones 4 and 5 are always pronounced as glides. ... There are also three more patterns that are combinations of two levels. One of these combinations begins at level 1 and rises to level 3; another begins at level 3 and falls to level 1; and another begins at level 3 and falls to level 2. These three combinations are indicated with the numbers 1-3, 3-1 and 3-2.
tn.cite: Hollenbach, Elena Erickson de [Barbara E.]. 2008. Gramática popular del triqui de Copala, San Juan Copala, Oaxaca. Serie de gramáticas de lenguas indígenas de México 11. México, D.F.: Instituto Lingüístico de Verano (versión electrónica 2010; SIL Mexico archives/35332).
tn.note: Five tone levels (1 lowest, 5 highest; 4 and 5 realised as glides) plus three two-level combinations 13, 31, 32: eight patterns, contrastive mainly on the final syllable; fixed final stress apart.

tn.quote: Length is characterised by a tonal lengthening of the vowel, best recognisable in first syllable position in bi- and multi-syllabic words: [doᵒʹmɛ] ‘Doms’, [ʔuᵘʹjar] ‘town’. 459.dq: At a most basic level, a phonological word can be classified simply by examining stress. As has already been seen, stress primarily occurs on the penultimate syllable. Postpositional enclitics, which bear no stress, are regularly attached to the final constituent in a noun phrase, or even to a postpostional phrase.
459.dloc: Bradshaw 2022, A grammar of Doromu-Koki (PhD thesis, JCU), sec. 2.8.1 'Structure of phonological word in contrast to grammatical word', p. 133
459.prule: Stress is not phonemic and falls on the penultimate syllable of words of two or more syllables (the sole syllable of monosyllables): ['bunĩ], [du'buinĩ], [bɑɾɑ'ɡinɑ̃], [ɑkhumõ'ɾoɾo], [bɑdɑmĩsi'ɾikhɑ]. It does not shift when an enclitic or a verbal suffix is added: enclitics bear no stress and a suffixed verb keeps stress on its stem (['jɑβɑ=ɾi] 'in/at the house', ['nĩ-bo-bi-ɡɛdi-mɑ̃] 'you (pl.) might be saying and then'). Members of compounds and reduplications each keep their own stress.
459.srule: Not mentioned in Bradshaw 2022 (sec. 2.5 'Prosodic features' pp. 125-126 and sec. 2.8.1 p. 133 read): one fixed penultimate stress per phonological word is described and words up to six syllables are transcribed with a single stress; the only multi-stress remark is that compounds and reduplications are two phonological words that 'maintain their individual stress' (p. 133).
